paragraphs.title: A Broken Spirit Surrounded by Mockery

easy.q: What does Job say about his spirit?
What does Job say about his days?

easy.explanation: Job asks, “Are there not mockers with me?”
easy.q: Who does Job say is with him?

answers: As his life fades, he says the graves are ready for him
medium.explanation: After saying that his days are extinct, Job says, “the graves are ready for me.”
medium.q: What connection does Job make between his fading life and the graves?

answers: People who are related to him
medium.explanation: Mockers are people who make fun of or ridicule someone.
medium.q: What does the word “mockers” mean in this passage?

answers: They are the only people surrounding Job
medium.explanation: Job presents the mockers as the people who are with him in his distress.
medium.q: Why is the presence of the mockers significant?

answers: A joyful man surrounded by friends
A man whose spirit is broken and who is surrounded by mockery
A man celebrating victory over his enemies
challenge.explanation: Job combines inner suffering with the presence of mocking people.
challenge.q: What overall picture emerges from the first two verses?

answers: His inward condition and outward treatment are both painful
The mockery has improved his condition
Job is unaware of what is happening around him
challenge.explanation: The verses show both personal suffering and distress caused by others.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Job’s corrupt breath and the mockers’ provocation?

answers: Job’s failing condition and the people provoking him
challenge.explanation: Job describes his own weakness while also describing the mockery around him.
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in these verses?

paragraphs.title: A Request for Guarantee and an Accusation Against His Friends

easy.explanation: Job says, “put me in a surety with thee,” speaking to God.
easy.q: From whom does Job ask for a guarantee?

answers: No one is willing to undertake his case
easy.explanation: He asks, “who is he that will strike hands with me?”
easy.q: What does Job imply about the people around him?

answers: Their hearts are hidden from understanding
easy.explanation: Job says, “thou hast hid their heart from understanding.”
easy.q: What does Job say about his friends’ understanding?

answers: To ask for protection and a pledge of support
To invite his friends to a feast
medium.explanation: A surety is someone who undertakes responsibility or guarantees protection.
medium.q: What is the purpose of Job’s request for a surety?

answers: Agree to undertake responsibility for me
medium.explanation: The expression refers to making an agreement or guaranteeing support.
medium.q: What does “strike hands with me” mean in this context?

answers: He asks God for what he does not receive from people
He asks his friends to praise God
He says that his friends have already protected him
medium.explanation: Job turns to God because he finds no human person willing to stand surety for him.
medium.q: How does Job’s request relate to his complaint about his friends?

challenge.explanation: Job criticizes their lack of understanding and their empty support.
challenge.q: What attitude toward his friends is evident in these verses?

answers: God is asked to guarantee him, while his friends are not seen as reliable protectors
His friends protect him, while God ignores him
God and his friends are presented in exactly the same way
challenge.explanation: Job asks God for a surety while questioning the reliability of those around him.
challenge.q: What contrast does Job make between God and his friends?

answers: Job believes he has many protectors
Job feels that no person is willing to undertake his cause
Job wants to punish all his friends
challenge.explanation: The question expresses Job’s loneliness and lack of human support.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the question, “who is he that will strike hands with me?”

paragraphs.title: Suffering That Turns Job into a Proverb

easy.explanation: Job says, “He hath made me also a byword of the people.”
easy.q: What has Job become to the people?

answers: It is dim because of sorrow
easy.explanation: Job says, “Mine eye also is dim by reason of sorrow.”
easy.q: What has happened to Job’s eye?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “The righteous also shall hold on his way.”
easy.q: Who will hold on his way?

answers: His body is like a shadow and his eye is dim
His body is strong and his sight is sharp
His body is at rest and his eyes are joyful
medium.explanation: Job says that his members are “as a shadow” and that his eye is dim.
medium.q: How does Job describe his body and his sight?

medium.explanation: The hypocrite is contrasted with the upright and innocent person.
medium.q: What does “hypocrite” mean in this passage?

answers: They continue in their way and grow stronger
medium.explanation: The righteous hold on their way, and those with clean hands become stronger.
medium.q: What does the passage say about the righteous and the innocent?

answers: They make him an object discussed and ridiculed by others
They make him a joyful storyteller
They cause him to forget his condition
challenge.explanation: Job says that he has become a public example and object of ridicule.
challenge.q: How do Job’s sufferings make him a “byword”?

answers: Both express physical weakness and decline
challenge.explanation: Both images emphasize Job’s failing physical condition.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Job’s dim eye and his body being like a shadow?

answers: Job’s weakness is set against the perseverance of the righteous
Day is contrasted with a feast
challenge.explanation: Job describes his own weakness while affirming that the righteous continue and grow stronger.
challenge.q: What major contrast appears in these verses?

paragraphs.title: Insulting the Friends, Passing Time, and Darkness

answers: He cannot find a wise man among them
They are all wiser than he is
easy.explanation: Job says, “I cannot find one wise man among you.”
easy.q: What does Job say about the wisdom of his friends?
What has happened to Job’s days?

easy.explanation: Job speaks of night, darkness, and light being overcome by darkness.

answers: His days pass, and his purposes and thoughts are broken off
Time stops and all his plans come true
Time restores all his former thoughts
medium.explanation: Job says both that his days are past and that his purposes and thoughts are broken off.
medium.q: What connection does Job make between passing days and his thoughts?

medium.explanation: Job’s purposes are the plans or intentions of his heart.
medium.q: What does “purposes” mean in this passage?

answers: The night is changed into day
The day completely removes the night
medium.explanation: Job says, “They change the night into day.”
medium.q: How are night and day described in verse 12?

answers: A sense that gloom has taken over Job’s life
A promise of an approaching celebration
challenge.explanation: Darkness dominates the passage and reflects Job’s despair.
challenge.q: What does the imagery of darkness communicate?

answers: He rejects their wisdom while feeling that his life and thoughts are falling apart
He praises them while describing their success
He asks them to measure the passing hours
challenge.explanation: Job joins his criticism of the friends with his sense of loss and mental distress.
challenge.q: How are Job’s criticism of his friends and his description of time related?

answers: Light is far removed from darkness
Light is present only briefly, while darkness remains dominant
Light has completely filled Job’s life
challenge.explanation: Even when light is mentioned, darkness limits and overshadows it.
challenge.q: What does “the light is short because of darkness” suggest?

paragraphs.title: Sheol as Home and the Loss of Hope

easy.explanation: Job says, “If I wait, the grave is mine house.”
easy.q: What does Job call his house?

easy.explanation: Job says, “I have said to corruption, Thou art my father.”
easy.q: To whom does Job say, “Thou art my father”?

easy.explanation: Job asks where his hope is and describes the grave as his expected dwelling.

answers: As his father, mother, and sister
medium.explanation: Job says to corruption, “Thou art my father,” and to the worm, “Thou art my mother, and my sister.”
medium.q: How does Job describe corruption and the worm?

answers: He has prepared to lie down in the grave and darkness
He has lit a lamp beside his bed
medium.explanation: Job uses the bed in darkness as an image of his expected resting place in the grave.
medium.q: What does “I have made my bed in the darkness” mean?

answers: Where is it, and who shall see it?
When will it defeat his friends?
medium.explanation: Job asks, “where is now my hope?” and “who shall see it?”
medium.q: What question does Job ask about his hope?

answers: He sees death as his near and expected dwelling
He expects to return home joyfully
challenge.explanation: Job speaks of the grave as his house and darkness as his bed.
challenge.q: What does the image of the grave as Job’s house reveal about his condition?

answers: Both are associated with descent into the grave and the dust
challenge.explanation: Job describes the worm as family and asks whether hope will descend with him to the grave.
challenge.q: How are family and hope connected in the closing passage?

answers: Going down to the pit and resting together in the dust
Walking from the grave back to his friends
challenge.explanation: The passage ends with going down to the bars of the pit and resting together in the dust.
challenge.q: What is the main movement described in the final verses?
